summary.en: A war from 1839 to 1842 between Britain and Qing China, which began when China took action against the British opium trade. The British fleet defeated the Chinese forces, and in the Treaty of Nanjing Britain gained Hong Kong Island and five ports opened to trade.

text.en: Wikipedia counts the war from the first battle at Kowloon on 4 September 1839, while Wikidata gives 18 March 1839 as the start. The end, 29 August 1842, matches.

intro.en: Opium was Britain's most profitable trade good in the 19th century, but the trade was banned in China. In 1839 the Daoguang Emperor sent the official Lin Zexu to Guangzhou (Canton) to stop it completely. Lin forced British merchants to hand over about 1,420 tonnes of opium and had it destroyed publicly at Humen in June. Tensions rose when drunken British sailors killed a Chinese villager in July and the British Superintendent of Trade Charles Elliot refused to hand them over.

members.en: The British Empire with the Royal Navy, British and Indian soldiers and the East India Company, under, among others, Charles Elliot, Hugh Gough and Henry Pottinger.
The Qing dynasty under the Daoguang Emperor, with officials and commanders such as Lin Zexu, Qishan, Yishan and Guan Tianpei.

outcome.en: The Treaty of Nanjing on 29 August 1842: China paid an indemnity, ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain and opened five ports to British merchants. The following year the British in China gained the right to be tried under their own laws. The treaty is among those the Chinese later called the unequal treaties. The unrest after the war lay behind the Taiping Rebellion, and in 1856–1860 a Second Opium War followed.

casualties.en: On the British side 87 were killed and 455 wounded, and 284 shipwrecked Indian sailors were executed or died in Chinese captivity. On the Chinese side about 3,100 are estimated to have been killed and 4,536 wounded, among them Manchu bannermen and their families who took their own lives at Zhapu and Zhenjiang. The figures are estimates.

summary.en: China has banned the sale of food to the British. On 4 September 1839 British boats open fire on Chinese war junks at Kowloon that are enforcing the ban. It is the war's first armed clash.

The British expeditionary fleet arrives in June 1840. On 5–6 July it takes the town of Dinghai on Zhoushan Island after a heavy bombardment from the ships, and the island becomes a base for the further operations along the coast.

On 7 January 1841 the British attack the forts at Humen at the mouth of the Pearl River, take them and destroy Chinese war junks. During the negotiations that follow, the British land on Hong Kong Island and raise the flag there on 26 January 1841.

On 21 July 1842 British troops storm Zhenjiang, where the Grand Canal meets the Yangtze. Manchu bannermen defend the city fiercely, and many soldiers and their families take their own lives rather than be captured. The British then cut the canal, which carried grain through the empire, and can sail on towards Nanjing.

With British warships ready to attack Nanjing, the peace treaty is signed on 29 August 1842 aboard HMS Cornwallis. China is to pay an indemnity, open five ports to British trade and cede Hong Kong Island to Britain. The war is over.

caption.en: The Treaty of Nanjing being signed and sealed. Engraving by John Burnet after a painting by Captain John Platt, published 1846. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: A major rebellion against the rule of the British East India Company in India. It began as a mutiny among Indian soldiers (sepoys) at Meerut and spread to further mutinies and civilian revolts, mainly in the Gangetic plain and central India. The rebellion was put down in 1858, and afterwards the British Crown took over the government of India.

title.en: About the name and the time

text.en: There is no name that everyone agrees on. In India and Pakistan it is often called the War of Independence of 1857 or the First Indian War of Independence, but also the Revolt of 1857. In Britain it has most often been called the Indian Mutiny or the Sepoy Mutiny. Some Indian politicians see the word mutiny as belittling, and the term war of independence is also criticised in India. Here the neutral term Indian Rebellion is used. Wikipedia gives the time as 10 May 1857–1 November 1858 (the amnesty) and Wikidata as 10 May 1857–20 June 1858 (the defeat at Gwalior).

intro.en: The East India Company ruled large parts of India on behalf of the British Crown. The discontent had many causes: social reforms on the British model, harsh land taxes, the treatment of wealthy landowners and princes, and doubts that Company rule made India richer. The Company had recently taken over princely states, Jhansi in 1853 and Awadh the year before the rebellion. Among the soldiers a rumour spread that the cartridges for the new Enfield rifle were greased with fat from pigs or cows, which offended both Muslims and Hindus. At Meerut, 85 soldiers who had refused to accept the cartridges were sentenced to long prison terms on 9 May 1857. The next day the garrison rose in revolt.

members.en: Sepoys from the Company's Bengal Army, the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar, who was proclaimed Emperor of Hindustan, Awadh with Begum Hazrat Mahal, Nana Sahib, Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Tatya Tope, Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur and many other groups of soldiers and civilians.

The East India Company and British troops, supported by princely states such as Patiala, Kapurthala and Nabha, Sikh princes in Punjab and the Kingdom of Nepal. Many Indians fought on the British side, and most remained calm.

outcome.en: The Company retook Kanpur in July and Delhi in September 1857, but it took most of 1858 to put down the rebellion in Jhansi, Lucknow and the countryside of Awadh. The rebellion was effectively over after the defeat at Gwalior in June 1858. On 1 November 1858 all rebels who had not murdered anyone were granted amnesty, but the war was formally declared over only on 8 July 1859. Bahadur Shah Zafar was convicted of treason and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862, and with that the Mughal dynasty came to an end. By an act in August 1858 the British Crown took over the government of India from the Company, and the Governor-General received the title of Viceroy.

casualties.en: About 6,000 of the roughly 40,000 Europeans in India were killed, among them civilians. The historian Peers estimates, from a rough comparison of uncertain population figures before 1857 and the 1871 census, that probably 800,000 Indians died, and probably more, in the rebellion and in the famine and epidemics that followed. In Awadh alone some estimates give 150,000 Indians killed, of whom 100,000 were civilians. Both sides committed atrocities against civilians.

summary.en: On 10 May 1857 the Indian soldiers of the Meerut garrison rise up and free 85 comrades who had been sentenced for refusing to accept the new cartridges. British officers and about twenty British civilians are killed, as are about 50 Indian civilians. During the night the rebels make their way to Delhi.

The rebels make Delhi their centre and proclaim the 81-year-old Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar Emperor of Hindustan. The Company's troops besiege the city from June and storm it on 14 September. After a week of street fighting Delhi is taken on 21 September 1857. The city is plundered and many inhabitants are killed.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the siege and Wikidata give 8 June–21 September 1857. Wikipedia's article on the rebellion says the siege lasted from about 1 July to 21 September.

caption.en: The Kashmiri Gate in Delhi with the damage from the fighting. Photograph by Samuel Bourne in the 1860s, a few years after the siege. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Sepoys under Nana Sahib besiege the Company's entrenchment at Cawnpore for three weeks. The besieged surrender on a promise of safe passage, but on 27 June most of the men are killed at the Ganges, and about 200 women and children are killed later at the Bibighar. When the Company's troops retake the city in July they take revenge on captured rebels and on civilians.

The Company's people and loyal sepoys defend the British Residency in Lucknow, the capital of Awadh, against the rebels for half a year. A first relief force arrives in September but is itself trapped. In November the defenders are evacuated by a larger army under Colin Campbell, and the Residency is abandoned.

The Company had taken over Jhansi in 1853, when the raja died without a biological son, and his widow Rani Lakshmibai became one of the leaders of the rebellion. The Company's army under Hugh Rose besieges the city from 24 March 1858 and takes it, but the rani flees on horseback.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 24 March–5 April 1858. Wikidata gives 23 March–2 April 1858. The year and the place match, but not the days.

summary.en: Rani Lakshmibai, Tatya Tope and other leaders have taken the fortress city of Gwalior from its prince, who was an ally of the Company. The Company's army attacks in mid-June 1858, and the rani is killed in the fighting. Gwalior is retaken within a few days. It is the rebellion's last major battle, but Tatya Tope continues with guerrilla warfare until he is captured and executed.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the rebellion says that the rani died on 17 June, the second day of the battle, and that the rebels were defeated on 20 June. The article on the rani says that the attack began on 17 June, that she died on 18 June and that the city was taken on 19 June. Wikidata gives 17 June as her date of death. The battle has no entry of its own in Wikidata.

summary.en: A war between Italy and Ethiopia in 1895–1896. Italy wanted to make Ethiopia a protectorate, but Emperor Menelik II rallied the whole country behind him, and at Adwa in 1896 the Ethiopian army defeated the Italians. Ethiopia remained independent, and the victory became a symbol for all of Africa.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 13 January 1895–23 October 1896, from the Battle of Coatit to the peace treaty. Wikidata gives the same end date but starts the war on 15 December 1894, when the rebellion in Akkele Guzay and the first fighting took place.

intro.en: Italy had taken Massawa on the Red Sea in 1885 and then the colony of Eritrea. In 1889 Emperor Menelik II concluded the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy, but the two language versions did not say the same thing. According to the Italian text, Ethiopia had to conduct its foreign affairs through Italy, which made the country an Italian protectorate. According to the Amharic text, Ethiopia was only to use Italy's embassy if it wished. Menelik denounced the treaty in 1893. The Italian prime minister Francesco Crispi wanted to build a colonial empire and chose a military solution. Italy counted on discontented princes going over to its side, but instead the Ethiopian leaders rallied behind the emperor. Menelik had for several years been buying modern rifles and cannon from, among others, France, Russia and even Italy. Russia was Ethiopia's only European ally.

members.en: Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu Betul, who herself commanded an army of her own at Adwa, with Ras Makonnen, Ras Mengesha Yohannes, Ras Alula, Ras Mikael, Welle Betul and Negus Tekle Haymanot of Gojjam. After Menelik's call to arms in September 1895, over 100,000 men gathered from all parts of the country. Thousands of women also took part, among other things as nurses and by providing food and water for the soldiers.

The Kingdom of Italy under Prime Minister Francesco Crispi, with General Oreste Baratieri as commander and the generals Dabormida, Arimondi, Ellena and Albertone. A large part of the soldiers were askari, African soldiers from Eritrea in Italian service.

outcome.en: Ethiopia won. After the defeat at Adwa, Crispi resigned within two weeks, and there were riots in several Italian cities. Menelik chose not to pursue the Italians into Eritrea. In the peace treaty of Addis Ababa in October 1896, Italy annulled the Treaty of Wuchale and recognised Ethiopia as fully independent, and the border with Eritrea was drawn up. Britain and France then concluded treaties of their own with Ethiopia as an equal. At the end of the 19th century Ethiopia was one of few independent countries in Africa and the only one that had won its independence through a military victory. The victory at Adwa became a rallying point for later African nationalists and for the Pan-African movement, and it is celebrated every year as a public holiday in Ethiopia. In Italy the defeat became a trauma, and in 1935 Italy attacked Ethiopia again.

casualties.en: The estimates differ. According to the source's compilation, 9,313 soldiers were killed on the Italian side (4,424 Italians and 4,889 askari), and 3,865 were taken prisoner. On the Ethiopian side about 10,000 were killed. At Adwa alone about 5,900–6,100 soldiers were killed on the Italian side and 3,886–7,000 Ethiopians, according to the historians Richard Caulk and George Berkeley. After the battle the Ethiopians punished about 800 captured Eritrean askari, whom they regarded as traitors, by cutting off their right hand and left foot, and many died of it. About 70 Italian prisoners were killed in revenge, but otherwise the Italian prisoners were generally treated better.

summary.en: On 13 January 1895 Italy's colonial army in Eritrea, where almost all the soldiers are Eritrean askari, meets Ras Mengesha Yohannes's Tigrayan army at Coatit. The Italians win the war's first battle and pursue Mengesha into Tigray, where they later take Adigrat, Adwa and Mekelle.

On 7 December 1895 the vanguard of Menelik's army, under Ras Makonnen, Ras Mengesha Yohannes and other commanders, attacks the Italian outpost on Mount Amba Alagi. The Italian force, mostly Eritrean askari under Major Pietro Toselli, is almost completely wiped out, and Toselli is killed. It is the first of the battles between Menelik's army and General Baratieri's.

Ethiopian troops surround the unfinished Italian fort at Mekelle, and in January 1896 Emperor Menelik and Empress Taytu arrive there with the main army. When the Ethiopians cut off the fort's water supply, the Italian force surrenders. Menelik lets the soldiers go free and even gives them pack animals.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the siege gives 7–21 January 1896 and says that the fort's commander raised the white flag on 19 January. The article on the war says that Ras Makonnen surrounded the fort on 18 December 1895 and that the commander agreed to surrender on 21 January. Wikidata gives 7–21 January 1896, like the article on the siege.

summary.en: On 1 March 1896 General Baratieri's Italian army, about 14,500–17,800 men, attacks the Ethiopian army at Adwa. The Italian brigades become separated from one another in the difficult terrain, and the army of Menelik and Taytu, 73,000–100,000 men, armed with modern rifles and quick-firing cannon, defeats them one by one. The victory secures Ethiopia's independence and becomes a symbol of African resistance to colonialism.

caption.en: The Battle of Adwa in an Ethiopian painting, made between 1965 and 1975 according to the museum, showing, among others, Saint George, Emperor Menelik, Empress Taytu and General Baratieri. Tropenmuseum collection. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: The peace treaty of Addis Ababa ends the war on terms that largely favour Ethiopia. Italy annuls the Treaty of Wuchale and recognises Ethiopia as an independent country, and the Italian prisoners of war may return home in exchange for Italy paying 10 million lire for their upkeep. Italy nevertheless keeps most of the areas it had taken beyond the Mareb and Belessa rivers.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the treaty and Wikidata state that it was signed on 26 October 1896, but the infobox in the same article and the article on the war give 23 October.

summary.en: A series of wars in 1803–1815 in which shifting coalitions of European states fought France under Napoleon. For a time France dominated large parts of Europe but was finally defeated. According to estimates, from just under 3 million up to 5 million soldiers died, many of them from disease.

title.en: About the start of the war

text.en: Historians do not agree on when the French Revolutionary Wars ended and the Napoleonic Wars began. Wikipedia mentions three possible start dates: Napoleon's coup d'état on 9 November 1799, Britain's declaration of war on 18 May 1803 and Napoleon's coronation as emperor on 2 December 1804. British historians sometimes count the whole period 1792–1815 as one war, in France the Revolutionary Wars are often counted together with the Napoleonic Wars, and German historians may call the War of the Second Coalition (1798/99–1801/02) the first Napoleonic war. The globe follows Wikipedia and Wikidata: 1803–1815, from the declaration of war to the Second Peace of Paris.

intro.en: The wars grew out of the French Revolution and the Revolutionary Wars of 1792–1802, when France had withstood several coalitions of Europe's monarchies. The Peace of Amiens brought a brief peace between Britain and France, but it did not last. Britain was irritated that Napoleon Bonaparte, then First Consul, annexed Piedmont and Elba, did not withdraw his troops from Holland and occupied Switzerland again. The British, for their part, delayed leaving Malta. After a British ultimatum, Britain declared war on France on 18 May 1803. Napoleon was crowned emperor in 1804 and then faced five coalitions, as well as wars on the Iberian Peninsula and in Russia. During the wars Russia also fought the Ottoman Empire, Iran and Sweden.

members.en: Britain, Austria, Russia, Prussia, Spain (from 1808), Portugal, Sweden and, from 1815, the United Netherlands, with several smaller states. The composition shifted: Russia was France's ally from the Peace of Tilsit in 1807 until 1812, and Austria and Prussia sent troops to Napoleon's campaign against Russia in 1812.
The French Empire with client states, among others the German states of the Confederation of the Rhine, the Kingdom of Italy and the Duchy of Warsaw, as well as Denmark–Norway and, until 1808, Spain.

outcome.en: The coalition won. After the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 France was invaded, Paris was taken in March 1814 and Napoleon was forced to abdicate and was exiled to Elba. He regained power in 1815 during the so-called Hundred Days, but was defeated at Waterloo and exiled to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821. The Second Peace of Paris on 20 November 1815 ended the wars, and the Congress of Vienna redrew Europe's borders. Prussia grew and became a great power, and Britain became the world's leading naval and trading power. Sweden lost Finland to Russia in 1809 but received Norway from Denmark at the end of the war. The wars also contributed to the colonies of Spain and Portugal in Latin America winning their independence.

casualties.en: According to estimates, more than 1.8 million soldiers died on the coalition side and more than 1 million on the side of France and its allies, of whom about 600,000 from disease. Other estimates give up to 5 million soldiers dead in Europe, disease included. The figures are uncertain and given as ranges, and civilian deaths are not included.

summary.en: On 21 October 1805 a British fleet under Vice-Admiral Nelson defeats a Franco-Spanish fleet. Eighteen French and Spanish ships are captured or destroyed, and the British lose none. Nelson is killed in the battle. Napoleon can never again challenge the British at sea or threaten invasion.

On 2 December 1805 Napoleon defeats a Russo-Austrian army. The battle was called the Battle of the Three Emperors, since Napoleon, Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II were present. The victory, often counted as Napoleon's greatest, ends the War of the Third Coalition.

On 14 October 1806 the French defeat two Prussian armies on the same day: Napoleon at Jena and Marshal Davout at Auerstedt. The Prussian army is crushed, and Napoleon marches into Berlin on 27 October.
On 14 June 1807 Napoleon wins a decisive victory over the Russian army under Bennigsen. After the battle France and Russia make peace at Tilsit in July 1807.

text.en: Russia still used the Julian calendar. Wikipedia gives 2 June (Julian) and 14 June 1807 (Gregorian). Wikidata gives 14 June (Gregorian).

summary.en: The Treaty of Fredrikshamn on 17 September 1809 ends the Finnish War between Sweden and Russia, which is part of the Napoleonic Wars. Sweden cedes Finland, which becomes a self-governing grand duchy in the Russian Empire.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 17 September 1809 (Gregorian calendar). Wikidata gives 5 September in the Julian calendar, which is the same day.

summary.en: On 5–6 July 1809 Napoleon wins a costly but decisive victory over the Austrian army under Archduke Charles. It was the largest battle in European history up to that time, and the Fifth Coalition collapses.

On 7 September 1812, during Napoleon's campaign against Russia, about a quarter of a million soldiers meet at Borodino. It becomes the bloodiest day of the wars. The battle is not decided, the Russians withdraw and the French take Moscow, but the campaign ends in catastrophe for Napoleon's army.

On 21 June 1813 a British, Portuguese and Spanish army under Wellington defeats the French army under King Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother. The victory eventually leads to France losing the war on the Iberian Peninsula, which had lasted since 1808.

On 16–19 October 1813 Austria, Prussia, Russia and Sweden, with the Swedish crown prince Charles John among the commanders, defeat Napoleon at Leipzig. About 560,000 soldiers take part, making it the largest battle of the wars. Napoleon has to retreat to France.

On 18 June 1815, after Napoleon's return from Elba, he is defeated by a British-led army under Wellington and a Prussian army under Blücher. It is Napoleon's last battle. He abdicates on 22 June and is exiled to Saint Helena.

caption.en: The Battle of Waterloo in a painting by William Sadler. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The peace agreement in Paris on 20 November 1815 marks the end of the Napoleonic Wars. France receives its borders from 1790, is to pay 700 million francs in indemnity and is partly occupied by the coalition's troops.

A civil war in 1861–1865 between the government of the United States (the Union, the “North”) and the Confederate States of America (the “South”), which had broken away in order to preserve slavery. The Union won, and four million enslaved African Americans became free. It is the war in which the most Americans have died.

title.en: About the end of the war

text.en: Wikipedia gives 26 May 1865, when the last major Confederate forces west of the Mississippi surrendered. Wikidata gives 9 April 1865, when Lee surrendered at Appomattox, which is often counted as the end of the war.

intro.en: The struggle over slavery had been going on for decades. When the Republican Abraham Lincoln, who wanted to stop the expansion of slavery, won the presidential election in 1860, seven slave states in the South broke away from the United States and formed the Confederate States of America. They took over federal forts and property in the South. The war began on 12 April 1861, when the Southern states shelled Fort Sumter in South Carolina. Afterwards four more states broke away from the United States.

members.en: The government of the United States under Abraham Lincoln, the free states and the border states of Missouri, Kentucky, Maryland and Delaware. About 2.2 million soldiers, among them, from 1863, freed slaves and other Black men in the United States Colored Troops.

Eleven Southern states under President Jefferson Davis, with General Robert E. Lee, about 750,000–1,000,000 soldiers. In Indian Territory several Indigenous peoples were divided: about 12,000 warriors fought for the Confederacy and fewer for the Union. The Cherokee Stand Watie was the only general from an Indigenous people in the Confederate army.

outcome.en: The Union won. Lee surrendered at Appomattox on 9 April 1865, Lincoln was assassinated on 14 April, and the last major Confederate forces surrendered on 26 May. The Confederacy was dissolved, and the 13th Amendment to the Constitution abolished slavery throughout the United States in December 1865. Large parts of the South's infrastructure were destroyed.

casualties.en: Estimates of soldiers killed: 620,000 according to 19th-century calculations, about 750,000 and perhaps up to 850,000 according to J. David Hacker in 2011, and 698,000 according to a new calculation in 2024 using complete censuses. In addition, about 50,000 free civilians (Nofi 2001) and at least 60,000 freed slaves died in epidemics, probably tens of thousands more (Downs 2012).

summary.en: On 12–13 April 1861 the South Carolina militia shells the federal Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor until the American garrison surrenders the fort. No one is killed in the battle, but it becomes the beginning of the Civil War.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 12–13 April 1861. Wikidata gives 12–14 April 1861 (the garrison left the fort on 14 April).

summary.en: On 21 July 1861 two inexperienced armies of about 18,000 men each meet about fifty kilometres from Washington, in the war's first major battle. The Confederates win when reinforcements arrive by train. In the South it is called the First Battle of Manassas.

On 17 September 1862 the Union army under George McClellan stops Lee's first invasion of the North. With over 22,000 dead, wounded and missing, it is the bloodiest day in United States history. The outcome gave Lincoln the opportunity to issue a preliminary Emancipation Proclamation on 22 September.

On 1 January 1863 President Lincoln declares that all enslaved people in the states that have rebelled are free. It applies to more than 3.5 of the 4 million enslaved people in the United States, and freedom follows the Union army as it advances. The abolition of slavery becomes a war aim, and freed slaves can enlist in the Union army.

text.en: The proclamation was issued on 1 January 1863. Wikidata gives 22 September 1862, when Lincoln issued a preliminary proclamation.

summary.en: On 1–3 July 1863 the Union army under George Meade repels Lee's invasion of the North at Gettysburg. With over 50,000 dead, wounded and missing, it is the bloodiest battle of the war, and it is usually regarded as the turning point of the war.

caption.en: Pickett's Charge at Gettysburg. Print by L. Prang & Co. after Thure de Thulstrup's painting, 1887, digitally restored by Adam Cuerden. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: After the siege that began on 18 May, the Confederate garrison at Vicksburg surrenders on 4 July 1863, the day after Gettysburg. Ulysses S. Grant's victory gives the Union control of the Mississippi River and splits the Confederacy in two.

After leaving the capital Richmond, Lee's army tries to make its way west but is hemmed in. On 9 April 1865 Lee surrenders to Grant at Appomattox Court House, and about 28,000 Confederate soldiers lay down their arms. More surrenders follow in May and June.

On 19 June 1865 the Union general Gordon Granger announces in Galveston that the Emancipation Proclamation applies in Texas, where there were an estimated 250,000 enslaved people. The day is celebrated today as Juneteenth. Slavery throughout the United States is abolished by the 13th Amendment in December 1865.

text.en: The date and place come from Wikipedia. Wikidata's entry for General Order No. 3 lacks a date and place.

summary.en: On 23 June 1865 Stand Watie (in Cherokee Degadoga, “stands on two feet”) signs a ceasefire with the Union at Doaksville. His First Indian Brigade consisted mostly of Cherokee, Muscogee and Seminoles, and he was the last Confederate general to surrender. The Cherokee Nation was divided: Watie led the pro-Confederate part, John Ross the pro-Union part.

text.en: The date and place come from Wikipedia (the articles on Stand Watie and on the Civil War). Wikidata has no entry of its own for the surrender.

summary.en: Latin America's bloodiest war between states, 1864–1870, between Paraguay and the Triple Alliance of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay. Paraguay lost a large part of its population, according to several estimates more than half, and had to give up disputed land.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 13 November 1864–8 April 1870 (with a note that a source is missing) and in the text 1864–1870. Wikidata gives 27 December 1864–1 March 1870. Here the war is counted from the capture of the Marquês de Olinda on 12 November 1864 to Solano López's death on 1 March 1870.

intro.en: Since independence from Spain and Portugal, the states around the Río de la Plata had quarrelled over borders and over traffic on the rivers. Paraguay, which reaches the sea only via the rivers, had built up a strong army under Carlos Antonio López and his son Francisco Solano López. When Brazil entered Uruguay in 1864 to support one side in a civil war, Solano López responded by seizing the Brazilian ship Marquês de Olinda and attacking Mato Grosso. When Paraguay then entered Argentine Corrientes, Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay concluded a secret alliance against Paraguay. Historians disagree about the causes: some highlight Solano López's ambitions, others the neighbouring countries' involvement in Uruguay and Paraguay.

members.en: The Empire of Brazil (about 139,000 soldiers, among them freed slaves and Black units), Argentina (about 30,000) and Uruguay (about 5,600) under the Colorado Party's Venancio Flores, as well as the Paraguayan Legion of exiled Paraguayans.

Paraguay under President Francisco Solano López. Most of the soldiers were of Indigenous descent and spoke Guaraní, and the war made them see the defence as the cause of all Paraguay. Towards the end slaves, old men and children were conscripted. Uruguay's Blanco Party was on Paraguay's side in 1864–1865.

outcome.en: Paraguay lost. Solano López was killed at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870. Paraguay lost almost 40 per cent of the land it had laid claim to: Brazil received the areas north of the Apa River and Argentina received Misiones and the land south of the Pilcomayo River. Brazilian and Argentine troops occupied Paraguay until 1876.

casualties.en: Paraguay's losses are highly disputed. Whigham and Potthast (1999) reckon that 60–70 per cent of the population died, out of 420,000–450,000 inhabitants before the war, so that only about 28,000 adult men remained. Another estimate is about 300,000 dead out of 500,000–525,000, while Reber (1988) argues that the figures are greatly exaggerated, with a lowest conceivable figure of 21,000. Most civilians died of starvation and disease. On the Allied side, according to estimates, about 50,000 Brazilian soldiers and 50,000 civilians died, 18,000 Argentine soldiers and 13,000 civilians, and 10,000 Uruguayans.

summary.en: On 12 November 1864 the Paraguayan vessel Tacuarí catches up with the Brazilian steamer Marquês de Olinda on the Paraguay River and forces it back to Asunción, where everyone on board is arrested, among them the new governor of Mato Grosso. It happens before any war has been declared, in response to Brazil's invasion of Uruguay. In December Paraguay attacks Mato Grosso.

text.en: The date and place come from Wikipedia. Wikidata's entry for the event lacks a date and place.

summary.en: On 1 May 1865, after Paraguay has entered Argentine Corrientes, Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay conclude a secret alliance in Buenos Aires. The treaty determines how the war is to be fought and what Paraguay is to lose afterwards. When the terms leak out, the Paraguayans' will to defend themselves is strengthened.

On 11 June 1865 the Brazilian fleet under Admiral Barroso destroys most of Paraguay's fleet on the Paraná River. The defeat prevents Paraguay from holding on to Argentine land, and the war begins to turn in the Allies' favour.

On 24 May 1866 about 25,000 Paraguayans attack the Allies' camp at Tuyutí, after the Allies have entered Paraguay. The attack is repelled. It is counted as the bloodiest battle in South American history: Paraguay loses about 13,000 dead and wounded, the Allies just over 4,000.

caption.en: Uruguayan soldiers in a trench at Tuyutí. Albumen print from the photo studio Bate y Cía., 1866. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 22 September 1866 about 5,000 Paraguayans under José E. Díaz defend the trenches at Curupayty against an attack by about 20,000 Argentines and Brazilians. The Allies lose over 4,000 men, the Paraguayans under a hundred, and the Allied advance comes to a halt.
The fortress of Humaitá, which blocked the way up the Paraguay River, falls in July 1868 after a long siege. The road to the capital Asunción lies open, and it is occupied on 1 January 1869.

text.en: Wikipedia's overview article and Wikidata state that Humaitá fell on 25 July 1868. The article on the siege gives 22 July 1867–26 July 1868, and Wikidata states that the siege began on 2 November 1867.

summary.en: On 16 August 1869 about 3,500 poorly armed Paraguayans, mostly boys aged between nine and fifteen, old men and wounded, face over 20,000 Brazilian and Argentine soldiers. In Guaraní the battle is called Acosta Ñu ñorairõ, and in Paraguay it is called the Children's Battle. Every year on 16 August Paraguay honours the dead children on Children's Day.

text.en: Wikidata gives the same date but no coordinates for the battle, only the town of Eusebio Ayala. The point here is the location of the town.

summary.en: After a guerrilla war lasting over a year, Brazilian troops catch up with Francisco Solano López and his last 400 men at Cerro Corá, 45 Swedish miles north-east of Asunción, on 1 March 1870. López is killed, and the war is over.
The Scot Alexander Bain receives a British patent on 27 May 1843 for an electric printing telegraph, a fax-type apparatus.

text.en: Wikipedia states that Bain received a British patent on 27 May 1843 for an electric printing telegraph of the fax type. The Dictionary of National Biography (1885) mentions only his chemical telegraph from 1843, without a patent date.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of 19th-century black-and-white newspaper engraving, not a historical image.

summary.en: Alexander Graham Bell, then a professor in Boston, receives a US patent for the telephone on 7 March 1876.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of 19th-century black-and-white newspaper engraving, not a historical image.

summary.en: A series of wars in Spain's American colonies, from Mexico in the north to Chile and the Río de la Plata in the south. They began when the Spanish monarchy collapsed after Napoleon's invasion in 1808 and ended with new independent states being formed. Spain kept only Cuba and Puerto Rico.

title.en: About the length of the war

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give 25 September 1808 – 29 September 1833: from the formation of the Central Junta in Spain after Napoleon's invasion to King Ferdinand VII's death, after which Spain gave up its plans to reconquer the colonies. The fighting in America began in 1810, and the major wars ended in 1825–1826, when the last Spanish strongholds fell (Callao in January 1826). Other works therefore use shorter ranges, for example 1808–1826 in the title of Humphreys and Lynch's book, to which Wikipedia refers.

intro.en: When Napoleon invaded Spain in 1808 and the king abdicated, juntas were formed that ruled in his name, first in Spain and then in America. From 1810 royalists, who wanted to keep the Spanish monarchy, and patriots, who wanted independent monarchies or republics, could not agree, and the fighting spread across the whole continent. The wars were also civil wars with social and ethnic divisions: in Mexico the priest Miguel Hidalgo built his army from the rural poor, in Venezuela the llaneros, plainsmen of mixed origin and enslaved people, first fought for the king against the white landowners, and in Upper Peru guerrilla groups allied themselves with Indigenous peoples.

members.en: Juntas and new states in the Río de la Plata, Chile, Venezuela and New Granada (Gran Colombia), Mexico and Peru, led by, among others, Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín and Antonio José de Sucre, with allies among the Indigenous peoples. Support from about 6,500 British volunteers and from the United States.

The Spanish Crown and the Spanish Americans who wanted to keep the monarchy, with allies among the Indigenous peoples. Europeans made up only about a tenth of the royalist armies in America; the rest were born there.

outcome.en: Spanish America was divided into independent states. After the victory at Ayacucho in 1824 the last Spanish strongholds fell in 1825–1826, but Spain did not give up its plans to reconquer the colonies until King Ferdinand VII died in 1833, and renounced the mainland in 1836. Creoles and mestizos took over most offices from the Spain-born, but the creoles remained at the top of society. Slavery was not abolished immediately, but in most countries only in the 1850s. Many Spaniards were forced to leave the countries.

casualties.en: It is unknown how many died. The estimates reported are about one million dead in total, of whom about 600,000 in New Spain (Mexico) and about 400,000 in New Granada, and about 150,000 fallen royalists. The patriots' losses are given as unknown. The figures are rough estimates.

summary.en: After a week of meetings, 18–25 May 1810, the viceroy in Buenos Aires is deposed and a local government, the Primera Junta, takes over on 25 May. It did not want to recognise the Regency Council in Spain, which in turn regarded the junta as rebellious.

On 16 September 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo rings the church bell in Dolores and calls for rebellion. It becomes the beginning of Mexico's War of Independence. Every year the cry is repeated on the evening before Mexico's Independence Day.
On 5 April 1818 Chilean and Argentine patriots under José de San Martín defeat the Spanish army near Santiago. The victory secures the independence of Chile's core territory.

On 7 August 1819 Venezuelan and New Granadan troops, with a British Legion, under Simón Bolívar defeat a royalist army. The viceroy flees the capital Santa Fe (Bogotá), and New Granada becomes independent, even though the fighting continues for several years.
On 24 June 1821 Simón Bolívar's army wins a decisive victory over the royalist forces. The battle secures Venezuela's independence within the new Republic of Gran Colombia.

On 24 August 1821 Agustín de Iturbide and the Spanish government's highest representative in Mexico, Juan O'Donojú, sign a treaty recognising Mexico as an independent empire. The Spanish government rejected the treaty and did not recognise Mexico's independence until 1836.
On 24 May 1822 patriots under Antonio José de Sucre defeat the royalist army at an altitude of about 3,500 metres above Quito. The area that became Ecuador becomes independent from Spain.

On 9 December 1824 Peruvian and Colombian patriots under Antonio José de Sucre defeat the viceroy's army, and the viceroy is taken prisoner. The battle decides the independence of Peru and in practice of South America, even though a few Spanish strongholds held out until 1826.

caption.en: The Battle of Ayacucho in a painting by Martín Tovar y Tovar (1827–1902). Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 23 January 1826 the royalists surrender the fortress of Real Felipe. They had refused to accept the capitulation after Ayacucho and had been under siege since 5 December 1824, and thousands of soldiers and civilian refugees had died of starvation and disease. With this, Spanish rule in South America is at an end.
A war between the British Empire and the Zulu Kingdom in present-day South Africa, from January to July 1879. The Zulu won at Isandlwana, but Britain won the war and then divided up the Zulu Kingdom.

intro.en: Britain wanted to unite the colonies, the Boer republics and the African kingdoms of southern Africa in a federation, and the independent Zulu Kingdom stood in the way. In 1878 a British commission ruled almost entirely in favour of the Zulu in a border dispute with the Boers. At the same time as the decision was read out, on 11 December 1878, the High Commissioner Bartle Frere, on his own initiative, delivered an ultimatum to King Cetshwayo: the Zulu army was to be disbanded and a British representative allowed to live in the country. In practice this would have cost the king his throne, and the government in London did not want war. Cetshwayo did not reply, and on 11 January 1879 British troops entered Zululand. According to the source, Cetshwayo had never intended to attack Natal, but wanted to defend his own country.

members.en: Britain with the colony of Natal: British soldiers, colonial troops and African auxiliary troops (the Natal Native Contingent, in which many were exiled Zulus), as well as volunteer Boers from the South African Republic. Commanders included Lord Chelmsford and later Garnet Wolseley.

King Cetshwayo kaMpande and the Zulu army, a militia of age regiments armed with spears, cowhide shields and some older rifles. Commanders included Ntshingwayo Khoza and Mnyamana Buthelezi. On the Zulu side there were also the abaQulusi in the north-west and the Swazi chief Mbilini waMswati.

outcome.en: Britain won at Ulundi on 4 July 1879, and the Zulu army was scattered. Cetshwayo fled but was captured on 28 August and taken to Cape Town. Wolseley divided Zululand into small kingdoms under chiefs chosen by the British (the source gives thirteen in one place and eleven in another), which led to civil war. Cetshwayo was allowed to return in 1883 but died shortly afterwards, and in 1887 Britain annexed Zululand. The defeats early in the war damaged the image of British invincibility and contributed to the fall of Disraeli's government in 1880.

casualties.en: According to one estimate (Knight and Castle), about 6,900 Zulu warriors died and at least 3,500 were wounded. On the British side about 1,900 died. The figures are estimates, and the Zulu losses are uncertain: for individual battles they are often given as ranges, for example 1,000–3,000 dead at Isandlwana.

summary.en: The ultimatum to King Cetshwayo has expired without a reply. On 11 January 1879 Lord Chelmsford's main column crosses the river at Rorke's Drift, and two more columns enter along the coast and in the north. The goal is the king's capital Ulundi (oNdini).

text.en: The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata, so the year and place could not be compared with a second, independent source. The information comes from Wikipedia.

summary.en: On 22 January 1879 a Zulu army of about 20,000 men under Ntshingwayo Khoza attacks the British camp at Isandlwana while Chelmsford is away with part of the column. Using their classic formation, the horns and chest of the buffalo, the Zulu warriors surround the camp. Over 1,300 on the British side are killed, and the Zulu lose 1,000–3,000 men. It was the Zulu Kingdom's greatest victory of the war and stopped the first invasion.

caption.en: Lieutenants Melvill and Coghill try to save the regiment's colours at Isandlwana. Illustration after John Charles Dollman in the newspaper The Graphic, 15 March 1879. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On the same afternoon as Isandlwana, 3,000–4,000 Zulu warriors from the reserve, without the king's orders, attack the British supply depot at Rorke's Drift. Just over 150 British soldiers and colonial soldiers defend the station, a mission station that belonged to the Church of Sweden, into the early hours of 23 January. The Zulu warriors finally withdraw.

On 28 March 1879 British horsemen under Redvers Buller attack the abaQulusi stronghold on Hlobane Mountain. When the main Zulu army approaches, the British retreat turns into a rout. The battle ends in a Zulu victory.

The day after Hlobane, on 29 March 1879, about 20,000 Zulu warriors attack Evelyn Wood's fortified camp at Kambula, even though Cetshwayo had told the army not to attack fortified camps. After five hours they withdraw. The British lose 29 dead and the Zulu 758–2,000. Many warriors then go home, and the British gain the upper hand in the war.

On 2 April 1879 a British relief column under Chelmsford repels a Zulu attack on its fortified camp. The next day the column reaches Eshowe, where Charles Pearson's troops had been besieged for two months.

Cetshwayo tries to negotiate peace, but Chelmsford wants to win before he is replaced by Garnet Wolseley. On 4 July 1879 the British defeat the main Zulu army at the capital Ulundi (oNdini) and burn the king's kraal. It is the last battle of the war.
Fusajiro Yamauchi founds Nintendo in Kyoto on 23 September 1889. From the beginning the company makes handmade hanafuda playing cards.

caption.en: Hanafuda cards of the mushibana type from Nintendo, early Shōwa period (1926–1945), several decades after the founding. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Eiffel Tower is built as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair in Paris. The structure itself is completed at the end of March 1889.

caption.en: The Eiffel Tower as the top is being installed, 15 March 1889 according to the caption on the photograph. Photograph, unknown photographer, from Gustave Eiffel's book La tour de trois cents mètres (1900). Cropped. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: On 6–24 March 1884 a French expeditionary corps of over 10,000 men attacks the Chinese Guangxi Army holding the town of Bắc Ninh in Tonkin. The French take the town and utterly defeat the Chinese army. The fighting is part of the undeclared hostilities before the Sino-French War, which breaks out in August the same year.

On 23 April 1899, during the Philippine–American War, the young Filipino general Gregorio del Pilar first halts an American cavalry unit at Quingua. When the Americans receive reinforcements, they win the second phase of the battle. The battle opens an American offensive in the provinces of Bulacan and Pampanga.

text.en: Wikipedia and Wikidata give the same date. Wikidata has no coordinate for the battle, so the point is the town of Plaridel (formerly Quingua) according to Wikidata.

summary.en: On 7 August 1826 the army of the Ashanti Empire under King Osei Yaw Akoto meets an alliance of peoples from the Gold Coast, among them the Fante, Ga, Akyem and Ada, supported by British, Danes and Dutch. The Ashanti lose, and the victory prevents the empire from taking control of the coast.

text.en: Wikipedia says only that the battle took place near Accra, and Wikidata has a date but no place. The point is the town of Dodowa according to Wikidata. Wikipedia's article on Dodowa has a coordinate east of the prime meridian, whereas Wikidata and the Historical Conflict Event Dataset place the town west of it.

summary.en: In March 1802 Jean-Jacques Dessalines's troops defend the fort of Crête-à-Pierrot against Napoleon's army under Charles Leclerc. The French lose many soldiers in the assaults. On 24 March, when food and ammunition run out, the defenders break out in the night. The French take the fort, but the battle is remembered in Haiti as a heroic epic.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the battle states that it began on 2 March 1802. Wikidata gives 4 March, and Wikipedia's article on the revolution speaks of a twenty-day siege up to 24 March. The end date and place agree in all the sources.

summary.en: On 6 May 1802 Toussaint Louverture, the revolution's best-known leader and himself born into slavery, rides into Cap-Français and recognises Leclerc's authority in return for a promise of amnesty. On 7 June he is arrested all the same and taken to France. He is held prisoner in Fort de Joux in the Jura Mountains without proper care and dies there on 7 April 1803. The war continues under Jean-Jacques Dessalines.

text.en: The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata, so the year and place could not be compared with a second, independent source. The information comes from Wikipedia.

summary.en: On 18 November 1803 Dessalines's army, with François Capois at the head, defeats the last French forces under Rochambeau outside Cap-Français. It is the last major land battle of the revolution. The next day the French agree to leave the colony.

On 1 January 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaims in Gonaïves the former colony of Saint-Domingue the independent state of Haiti. It becomes the first independent state in Latin America, and the only one founded after a successful slave revolt.

caption.en: Haiti's declaration of independence, printed in 1804. The copy is held in the British National Archives (MFQ 1/184). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Abraham Lincoln, later President of the United States, is born on 12 February 1809 in LaRue County, Kentucky.

caption.en: Abraham Lincoln photographed by Alexander Gardner on 8 November 1863, 54 years after his birth. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Charles Darwin, who later formulates the theory of evolution by natural selection, is born in Shrewsbury on 12 February 1809.

caption.en: Charles Darwin photographed by Herbert Rose Barraud in 1881, long after his birth in 1809. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: A series of wars in 1845–1872 between New Zealand's colonial government, British troops and Māori who sided with the government, and Māori iwi (tribes) who defended their land and their self-government. In Māori they are called Ngā pakanga o Aotearoa; earlier they were also known as the Land Wars or the Māori Wars. The war ended with the government confiscating large areas of land from the Māori.

text.en: The sources date the war differently. Wikipedia and Wikidata give 1845–1872. The first armed clash between Māori and settlers, the Wairau Affray in June 1843, is sometimes included, and Wikipedia's article on Te Kooti's War therefore writes 1843–1872. Store norske leksikon writes that the Land Wars lasted from 1860 to 1865 but that the conflict flared up again several times until the end of the 19th century, and the Danish encyclopaedia Lex writes that the actual wars were fought in 1862–1870. On the confiscated land, Wikipedia's article on the war gives 1.5 million hectares, roughly 15 per cent of the land then owned by Māori, whereas the article on the confiscations gives more than 1.2 million hectares, 4.4 per cent of the land. On troop strength, Wikipedia says both that 18,000 British soldiers fought in the 1860s when the fighting was at its most intense and that the force at its largest was about 14,000 men in March 1864, of whom 9,000 were British. An older Māori name for the war is te riri Pākehā, “the white man's anger”.

intro.en: The Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 gave the Crown the exclusive right to buy Māori land, but the English and the Māori texts said different things: in English the chiefs ceded sovereignty, while in Māori the word was translated as kawanatanga, “governance”. Many Māori wanted to keep their self-determination, tino rangatiratanga. As more and more settlers arrived, the government wanted to buy more land, and disputes over contested land purchases turned into war. In the north the Ngāpuhi chief Hōne Heke cut down the British flagstaff at Kororāreka. From 1860, after a disputed purchase at Waitara, the government was convinced that it faced united Māori resistance to land sales, and it launched large campaigns against the Kīngitanga movement. Later fighting concerned the religious movements Pai Mārire and Ringatū and the leaders Tītokowaru and Te Kooti.

members.en: The British Army and Navy, the New Zealand militia, volunteers and the special force the Forest Rangers, at least 2,500 volunteers from the Australian colonies and the warships of the colony of Victoria, as well as kūpapa: Māori who fought on the government's side, for example Tāmati Wāka Nene and most of the Ngāpuhi in the north, and Ngāti Porou and Te Arawa in the later fighting.

Among others the Ngāpuhi under Hōne Heke and Te Ruki Kawiti in the north, Te Āti Awa under Wiremu Kīngi in Taranaki, the Kīngitanga (the Māori King movement) with Ngāti Maniapoto under Rewi Maniapoto and Ngāti Hauā under Wiremu Tamihana, Ngāi Te Rangi in Tauranga, Tūhoe, Ngāruahine under Tītokowaru and Te Kooti's followers. According to the historian James Belich, at least 4,000 warriors were mobilised, a third of the men able to bear arms.

outcome.en: The Crown won militarily but seldom achieved the decisive victories it sought, and Māori fortifications (pā) dealt British troops several heavy defeats. From 1863 the government, under the New Zealand Settlements Act, confiscated about 1.5 million hectares of land in Taranaki, Waikato, Tauranga and the Bay of Plenty, roughly 15 per cent of the land then owned by Māori, both from tribes that had resisted and from those that had been loyal. The Waitangi Tribunal has criticised the Crown's conduct in several reports, and the Crown has formally apologised to several iwi in settlements of historical claims. Since 2017 a national day of remembrance has been held on 28 October.

casualties.en: According to Wikipedia, about 1,800 Māori and 800 Europeans died during the campaigns in Taranaki and Waikato, and Māori losses in all the wars may have been over 2,100. Civilians were also killed, including women and children at Ōrākau in 1864 and 51 men, women and children when Te Kooti's forces attacked Matawhero in 1868. In 2013 the Waitangi Tribunal estimated that the East Coast lost about 43 per cent of its male population in the war of 1865–1869. The figures are estimates.

summary.en: On 11 March 1845 Ngāpuhi warriors under Hōne Heke and Te Ruki Kawiti attack the town of Kororāreka. Heke had already cut down the British flagstaff several times, in protest at how the 1840 treaty was being applied. The British evacuate the town, which largely burns down. The Flagstaff War in the north has begun.

caption.en: Kororāreka (today Russell) seen from the sea before the attack of 1845, with three ships in the foreground. Image from 1845 in the National Library of New Zealand. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Te Ruki Kawiti has built Ruapekapeka, a fortified pā with underground shelters that withstand cannon fire. After about two weeks of siege, British troops take the almost empty fortification on 11 January 1846. Heke and Kawiti then make peace with Governor George Grey, and Ngāpuhi land is not confiscated.

title.en: Only one source for the date

text.en: Wikidata confirms the place but gives no date for the battle, so the dates rest only on Wikipedia. Wikidata gives the same end date, 11 January 1846, for the whole Flagstaff War.

summary.en: Governor Thomas Gore Browne approves the purchase of the Pekapeka land at Waitara, even though the Te Āti Awa chief Wiremu Kīngi Te Rangitāke has said no. On 17 March 1860 British troops bombard Kīngi's pā. The Taranaki war ends after a year in a truce. In 1996 the Waitangi Tribunal concluded that the government was the aggressor.

On 20–21 November 1863 more than 1,400 British soldiers defeat about 500 warriors of the Kīngitanga, the Māori King movement, in the battle that cost both sides the most lives in the wars. 180 Māori are taken prisoner. In 1995 the Crown apologised for its conduct.

caption.en: The Royal Navy storming party is repulsed at the pā at Rangiriri on 20 November 1863. Drawing by Charles Heaphy, from James Cowan’s The New Zealand Wars (1922). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: About 200–250 warriors, mainly Tūhoe and Ngāti Raukawa, and about 50 women and children defend a newly built pā against up to 1,800 British and colonial soldiers for three days. Rewi Maniapoto is said to have answered the call to surrender: “Ka whawhai tonu ahau ki a koe, ake, ake” (“I will fight against you for ever”). On 2 April the besieged break out; many are killed during the flight, including women and children. Ōrākau became the best-known battle of the wars.

text.en: The dates rest only on Wikipedia; Wikidata has no entry for the battle. The place is the town of Ōrākau according to Wikidata. Estimates of the Māori dead vary between 80 and 160.

caption.en: Survivors from Ngāti Maniapoto at the fiftieth anniversary on the battlefield at Ōrākau on 1 April 1914. All but one of them took part in defending the pā. Photograph from James Cowan's The New Zealand Wars (1922). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 29 April 1864 about 230 warriors, mainly Ngāi Te Rangi under Rawiri Puhirake, defend the fortification at Pukehinahina against about 1,650 British soldiers. After eight hours of bombardment the British storm it but are beaten back from hidden trenches. It was the British's worst defeat in the wars, but seven weeks later Ngāi Te Rangi were defeated at Te Ranga.

text.en: The date rests only on Wikipedia; Wikidata has no entry for the battle. The place is the suburb of Gate Pā according to Wikidata.

caption.en: British soldiers and Māori in battle at Gate Pā in 1864. Later illustration, published in 1895 in a British book (Archibald Forbes, Arthur Griffiths and others). Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The spiritual leader Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Turuki has been hunted for four years by government troops and Māori forces. The last shots of the New Zealand Wars are fired on 14 February 1872. On 15 May 1872 Te Kooti crosses the Waikato River and receives asylum with the Māori King Tāwhiao. He is pardoned in 1883.

In Tasmania the Indigenous peoples have put up fierce resistance to the settlers since the mid-1820s. On 7 October 1830, 2,200 soldiers, convicts and settlers march out in a chain more than 300 kilometres long to drive them away from the colonised areas. The attempt fails and is called off on 26 November. After negotiations through George Augustus Robinson and Indigenous mediators such as Truganini and Mannalargenna, the last groups surrender in January 1832, and the survivors are taken to Flinders Island.

text.en: The dates rest only on Wikipedia. Wikidata has no entry of its own for the Black Line, but gives the 1820s to 1832 for the whole war in Tasmania. The historian Lyndall Ryan proposes the name “Tasmanian War” instead of “Black War”.

summary.en: On 28 October 1834 Governor James Stirling, with 25 soldiers, police and settlers, attacks a camp of 60–80 Bindjareb Noongar by the Murray River. Stirling stated that about 15 men were killed, an eyewitness counted 25–30 dead, among them a woman and several children, and Bindjareb oral history gives more. The event was formerly called “the Battle of Pinjarra”.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the massacre and Wikidata give 28 October 1834. Wikipedia's overview article on the frontier wars gives 28 October 1833.

summary.en: On 10 June 1838 a group of armed stockmen kill at least 28 unarmed Wirraayaraay, part of the Kamilaroi people, who had sought shelter at Myall Creek station. It was one of the few massacres of Aboriginal people to be tried in court: after two trials, seven of the perpetrators were convicted of murder and hanged, while the leader was never brought to trial.

caption.en: “Australian Aborigines slaughtered by convicts”, illustration by Hablot Knight Browne (Phiz) in The Book of Remarkable Trials, 1840, two years after the massacre. The title of the picture does not mention the place, but a later adaptation of the image on Wikimedia Commons describes it as the scene at Myall Creek. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Rather than face Kamehameha's great fleet, Kauaʻi's king Kaumualiʻi negotiates a peaceful solution. In Honolulu in 1810 he recognises Kamehameha as supreme ruler. Kauaʻi and Niʻihau become tributaries of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, and Kaumualiʻi is allowed to continue ruling the islands.

text.en: The event rests only on Wikipedia. The article on Kamehameha I gives April 1810, the article on Kaumualiʻi only the year.

summary.en: A civil war in China between the Qing dynasty and the rebel Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, fought mainly along the Yangtze River. It is regarded as the deadliest civil war in history. Most estimates put the dead at 20–30 million, but some go as high as 100 million.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the war began in December 1850, with a minor battle before the uprising in Jintian. Wikidata gives 11 January 1851 as the start date but December 1850 as the point in time. Both give August 1864 as the end, a month after the fall of Nanjing. Fighting with remaining Taiping forces continued until 1866, and the last Taiping army was defeated in 1871.

intro.en: China's population had almost doubled between 1766 and 1833 without any increase in farmland, and Qing rule was weak in the south. Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka from Guangdong who had failed the civil service examination several times, interpreted his visions with the help of Christian scriptures and saw himself as the younger brother of Jesus. His movement, the Society of God Worshippers, grew in Guangxi. When the authorities moved against it, it rose in revolt, in January 1851 at Jintian. The aim was to overthrow the Qing dynasty and transform the whole of society.

members.en: The Qing emperor with the regular armies (the Eight Banners and the Green Standard Army) and provincial armies such as the Xiang Army under Zeng Guofan and the Huai Army under Li Hongzhang. In the later stages support from Britain and France, and the Western-led Ever Victorious Army.

The Taiping army under Hong Xiuquan and leaders such as Yang Xiuqing, Shi Dakai, Li Xiucheng and Chen Yucheng. At times cooperation with other rebel movements, such as the Nian rebels, the Red Turbans and the Small Swords Society.

outcome.en: The Qing dynasty won. Hong Xiuquan died in June 1864 and Nanjing fell in July the same year. The victory cost the dynasty dearly: the economy and central power were weakened, and the provincial armies and leaders gained more power. The rebellion also led to the Self-Strengthening Movement, an attempt to modernise China.

casualties.en: No reliable census exists, so the figures are uncertain. The most cited estimates are 20–30 million dead soldiers and civilians, about 5–10 per cent of China's population. Other estimates go as high as 73–100 million. Most died of starvation and epidemics. About 30 million people fled.

summary.en: On 11 January 1851 Hong Xiuquan proclaims the uprising at Jintian and founds the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, with himself as Heavenly King. His followers have just repelled Qing troops who attacked them. It marks the beginning of the war.

On 19 March 1853 the Taiping army conquers Nanjing after a siege of just under two weeks. Hong Xiuquan makes the city his capital and calls it Tianjing, “the Heavenly Capital”. The Manchu garrison and its families are killed.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of Chinese ink painting on a silk scroll, not a historical image.

summary.en: On 8 May 1853 a Taiping army sets out from Yangzhou to take Beijing. It advances towards Tianjin in the autumn but cannot cope with the North China winter and is forced to turn back. By 1855 almost the entire army has been annihilated.

text.en: Wikipedia gives both 31 March and 31 May 1855 for the end of the expedition. Wikidata gives only the years 1853–1855 and the place China. The point on the map shows roughly how far north the army got.

summary.en: From 2 September 1856 the Taiping leaders fight one another in the capital. Yang Xiuqing, Wei Changhui and Qin Rigang are killed, along with more than 27,000 others. The fighting weakens the movement and is usually seen as a turning point in the war.

From September 1860 Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army besieges the Taiping-held city of Anqing on the Yangtze. On 5 September 1861 the troops break through the walls. The way down the river towards Nanjing is thus open.

Taiping armies try in 1861–1862 to take the port city of Shanghai. Qing troops, the Huai Army, the Western-led Ever Victorious Army and British and French forces repel the attacks, and the Taiping give up their plans for the city.

text.en: In different places Wikipedia gives June 1861–July 1862, July 1861–November 1862, and that the attack was repelled after 15 months. Wikidata gives July 1861–November 1862.

summary.en: From 14 March 1864 the Qing army attacks the encircled capital. Hong Xiuquan dies on 1 June, and on 19 July the attackers blow up part of the wall and take the city after fierce street fighting. The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom is thereby defeated, even though scattered fighting continues for a few years.

A convention at Washington-on-the-Brazos adopts the Texas Declaration of Independence from Mexico on 2 March 1836, in the midst of the Texas Revolution. The Republic of Texas then exists for just under ten years, until it becomes a US state.

caption.en: The Texas Declaration of Independence from 1836. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 17 January 1893 the chairman of the Committee of Safety reads out a proclamation in front of ʻIolani Palace in Honolulu: Queen Liliʻuokalani is deposed, the monarchy abolished and a provisional government appointed. At the committee's request the US envoy has sent American marines ashore. The Kingdom of Hawaiʻi had existed since 1795.

caption.en: Queen Liliʻuokalani leaves Aliʻiōlani Hale in Honolulu in 1893. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The British Parliament passes a law banning the slave trade across the Atlantic throughout the British Empire, after 18 years of attempts. The law receives royal assent on 25 March 1807 and takes effect on 1 May. It does not free those who are already enslaved; slavery remains legal in most of the empire until 1833. British ships had until then carried about a third of all enslaved people across the Atlantic, roughly 3.5 million people. Behind the ban lay both campaigns in Britain and the resistance of the enslaved themselves: revolts on board ship and in the Americas drove the debate forward. The trade continued illegally, and over a quarter of all those carried across the Atlantic were shipped after 1807.

On 13 May 1888 Princess Isabel, who is ruling in place of her father Emperor Pedro II, signs the Lei Áurea, the Golden Law. It abolishes slavery in Brazil, which becomes the last country in the Americas to do so. Brazil received more enslaved Africans than any other country. The enslaved resisted throughout, among other things by escaping and forming communities of their own, quilombos, such as Palmares.

text.en: How many were brought to Brazil is uncertain. Wikipedia's article on slavery in Brazil writes about 5.5 million between 1540 and the 1860s, while the article on the Lei Áurea reckons 40 per cent of 10 million, that is about 4 million.

caption.en: The Lei Áurea, the law that abolished slavery in Brazil in 1888. Licence: CC0.

summary.en: After US President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act on 28 May 1830, about 60,000 people from the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw nations are forced out of their homelands in the south-eastern USA to Indian Territory west of the Mississippi River. The Choctaw are forced first, in 1831, and the Cherokee last: in May 1838 the army is ordered to remove them, and in the winter of 1838–1839 they walk about 1,600 kilometres, most of them on foot. Thousands die of disease, starvation and cold on the way or shortly afterwards. Scholars describe the removal as ethnic cleansing or genocide.

text.en: In its running text Wikipedia writes that about 4,000 Cherokee died during the march, but in its table the same article gives 4,000–8,000 dead for the Cherokee. The table also gives 2,000–4,000 or more dead among the Choctaw, 3,500–4,500 among the Muscogee and 500–800 among the Chickasaw.

summary.en: After the Berlin Conference, King Leopold II of Belgium gets the European powers to recognise him as ruler of almost the whole Congo Basin, an area of 2.35 million square kilometres. The Congo Free State is his private property, not Belgium's, and he never visits it. The people are forced to collect wild rubber and ivory, and the army, the Force Publique, and the concession companies punish with murder, flogging, burned villages and severed hands. Together with diseases such as sleeping sickness, starvation and flight, the population falls sharply. Missionaries' testimony and Roger Casement's report in 1904 prompt an international protest, and in 1908 Belgium takes over the territory as a colony, the Belgian Congo.

text.en: How much the population fell is disputed: modern estimates lie between 1.2 and 10 million people, and scholars disagree on whether the abuses should be called genocide. The dates also differ: Leopold announced the name on 29 May 1885, Wikipedia and Wikidata give 1 July 1885 as the beginning, and the name officially replaced the old one on 1 August. Wikipedia states that Belgium took over on 15 November 1908, Wikidata on 2 April 1908.

summary.en: On 6 December 1865, 27 states have ratified the Thirteenth Amendment to the US Constitution, and it thereby takes effect. The amendment prohibits slavery and involuntary servitude throughout the USA, except as punishment for someone convicted of a crime. The two chambers of Congress had passed the amendment in 1864 and in January 1865.

caption.en: The celebration in the House of Representatives when Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment. Print in Harper's Weekly, 18 February 1865. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 3 January 1868 the Tokugawa shogunate is overthrown, and imperial power is restored in Japan under Emperor Meiji. The Empire of Japan is formed. The domains are dissolved, the samurai lose their position as a class and the feudal system is abolished. Japan industrialises and follows Western models.

caption.en: The Emperor's procession to Tokyo crosses the Rokugo River, autumn 1868. Woodblock print by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi from the same year. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 17 November 1869 the Suez Canal opens between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Construction began on 25 April 1859 and was carried out by a company formed by Ferdinand de Lesseps to build the canal. The canal becomes an important trade route between Europe and Asia, since ships no longer need to sail around Africa.

caption.en: The inauguration of the Suez Canal on 17 November 1869. Picture by Édouard Riou from the same year. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 27 August 1883 the volcanic island of Krakatoa has its most powerful eruption. The third explosion is the loudest sound known. The eruption and the tsunamis it causes kill at least 36,417 people. The following year, summers in the Northern Hemisphere are on average 0.4 °C colder.

caption.en: The eruption of Krakatoa in 1883, photographed by an unknown photographer. The surviving copy is a photograph of a photograph. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885, 14 parties from Europe, the USA and the Ottoman Empire meet in Berlin. The German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck has issued the invitation at the request of King Leopold II of Belgium. No African countries are invited. The final act regulates how the European powers colonise and trade in Africa and recognises Leopold's territory in the Congo. It can be seen as formalising the Scramble for Africa, but some historians argue that the conference's role is often exaggerated.

caption.en: The delegates at the Berlin Conference. Drawing by Adalbert von Roessler in the magazine Über Land und Meer, 1884. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 19 September 1893 the governor, Lord Glasgow, signs an electoral act giving women over 21 the right to vote. New Zealand becomes the first country in the world where all women can vote in parliamentary elections. Behind the reform were, among others, Kate Sheppard and petitions that in 1893 received nearly 32,000 signatures. Women vote for the first time on 28 November 1893, but they cannot be elected to parliament until 1919.

caption.en: The 1893 petition for women's suffrage, photographed at Archives New Zealand long afterwards. Licence: CC BY-SA 2.0.

summary.en: On 6–15 April 1896 the first modern Olympic Games are held in Athens. They are organised by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which Pierre de Coubertin created at a congress in Paris in 1894. According to the IOC, 14 countries and 241 athletes take part, all men, but both figures are interpreted differently. The opening and closing ceremonies are held at the Panathenaic Stadium.

caption.en: The opening of the first modern Olympic Games in Athens in 1896. Photo by an unknown photographer, reproduced in a French magazine in 1928. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 10 April 1815 the eruption of the volcano Tambora on the island of Sumbawa reaches its most violent phase. It is regarded as the most powerful volcanic eruption in humanity's recorded history. About 10,000–11,000 people die directly from the eruption and 49,000–90,000 from the starvation and disease afterwards; other estimates are higher or lower. The cooling causes 1816 to be called the Year Without a Summer, with extreme weather and crop failures in many parts of the world.

caption.en: The crater of the volcano Tambora on Sumbawa, photographed in 2017. Contemporary photo. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: On 15 September 1830 the railway between Liverpool and Manchester opens, the world's first railway between two cities. It is also the first to use only steam locomotives and the first with a fixed timetable. The locomotive Rocket had been designed by George Stephenson and his son Robert. On the opening day the Member of Parliament William Huskisson is killed.

caption.en: The opening of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830. Print after I. Shaw junior. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 6 February 1840 Captain William Hobson, for the British Crown, and Māori chiefs sign the Treaty of Waitangi at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands. About 530–540 Māori sign the Māori version but only 39 the English one. The texts differ: the English one cedes sovereignty to the Crown, whereas the Māori one gives the Crown kawanatanga, governance. The treaty is increasingly seen as New Zealand's founding document, and 6 February is the national day.

caption.en: The Waitangi Sheet, one of the copies of the Treaty of Waitangi from 1840. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 24 November 1859 the publisher John Murray in London issues Charles Darwin's book On the Origin of Species. Darwin shows that populations change over generations through natural selection. On 1 July 1858 papers by Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace on evolution had been read at the Linnean Society in London. The book is regarded as the foundation of evolutionary biology.

caption.en: The title page of the first edition of Darwin's On the Origin of Species, John Murray 1859. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 7 September 1822 Prince Regent Pedro of Braganza declared Brazil independent from Portugal, by the Ipiranga brook in São Paulo. The event is called the Cry of Ipiranga and the day is celebrated as Brazil's national day. Pedro was proclaimed emperor in October the same year, and the country became the Empire of Brazil. A war against the Portuguese forces followed, and the last Portuguese soldiers left the country in 1824. Portugal recognised Brazil's independence in a treaty on 29 August 1825.

At the end of February 1848 the Communist Manifesto was published in London, without an author's name and in German, as a 23-page pamphlet. It was written by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels on commission from the Communist League. The text describes history as a struggle between social classes and criticises how workers are exploited under capitalism. It appeared at the same time as the revolutions of 1848 in Europe and has become one of the world's most influential political texts.

caption.en: The title page of the Communist Manifesto, printed in London and, according to the page itself, published in February 1848. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Marie Curie examined the uranium mineral pitchblende and saw that it radiated more than uranium itself, which indicated that it contained an unknown and more active substance. She and her husband Pierre Curie worked in a converted shed next to the ESPCI school in Paris. In July 1898 they announced that they had found a new element, which they called polonium after her homeland Poland. On 26 December 1898 they announced a second element, radium. During the work they also coined the word radioactivity.

caption.en: Pierre and Marie Curie in the laboratory, photographed around 1904. Photographer unknown. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Sokoto Caliphate was founded in 1804 by Usman dan Fodio during the Fulani jihads, after he had fled from the Hausa king Yunfa. In 1808 the caliphate controlled the Hausa lands. By 1837 it had 10–20 million inhabitants and was West Africa's most populous state. In 1903 British, French and German forces conquered the area.

On 26 July 1847 Liberia's constitutional convention adopted the declaration of independence and the country's first constitution. The colony had been founded by the American Colonization Society for freed African Americans and now became the Republic of Liberia. The declaration lists the injustices to which African Americans had been subjected during slavery in the USA. The day is celebrated as Liberia's Independence Day.

On 16 November 1855 the missionary David Livingstone became the first European known to have seen the waterfall on the Zambezi River. He called it Victoria Falls after Queen Victoria. The falls had long been known to the peoples of the area, and the Lozi name Mosi-oa-Tunya, “the smoke that thunders”, is still used. Both names appear on the World Heritage List.

In the 1890s the rinderpest virus spread across Africa, mainly in the east and south. South of the Zambezi more than 5.2 million cattle died, and wild animals such as buffalo and giraffe were also affected. It led to famine: according to estimates, a third of Ethiopia's population and two thirds of the Maasai people in Tanzania died. The disease had been introduced with infected cattle from Asia, which were to feed the Italian troops during the war between Italy and Ethiopia in 1887–1889.

On 20 August 1860 the Burke and Wills expedition left Royal Park in Melbourne, watched by about 15,000 people. Nineteen men under Robert O'Hara Burke were to cross Australia to the Gulf of Carpentaria in the north, about 3,250 km, with horses, wagons and 26 camels. Burke, Wills and two others came close to the north coast, but on the return journey Burke and Wills died around 30 June 1861. Only John King crossed the continent and came back alive.

caption.en: Burke, Wills and King on the way back from the Gulf of Carpentaria. Engraving by Nicholas Chevalier, before 1868. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: From 1851 to the end of the 1860s gold was found in several places in the colony of Victoria, including Ballarat, Bendigo, Castlemaine, Daylesford and Beechworth. People flocked there and Melbourne became very rich. In the record year 1856 almost 95 tonnes of gold were mined. The gold diggers pushed for more democracy, but Chinese gold diggers met with riots and special taxes, something that became a basis for the White Australia policy.

On 22 August 1872 the two sections were joined at Frew's Ponds, and the telegraph line across Australia was complete, more than seven months late. The line ran about 3,200 km between Darwin and Adelaide, and the work was led by Charles Todd.
