When it was connected a few months later to the submarine cable from Java, the time for a message to reach Europe shrank from months to hours.

On 10 October 1874 Fiji became a British crown colony with Levuka as its capital. The chief Seru Epenisa Cakobau had offered the islands to the British as early as 1852 but was refused. Debts and threats from the US Navy led him in 1871 to introduce a constitutional monarchy, and when it collapsed he offered again in 1872 to cede the islands. The colony lasted until independence in 1970.

Early in the morning of 10 June 1886 the volcano Tarawera near Rotorua had a violent eruption that lasted about six hours. About 120 people died, and it is New Zealand's largest and deadliest eruption in the past 500 years. Ash covered villages such as Te Wairoa, and the famous Pink and White Terraces, the country's best-known tourist attraction, are believed to have been destroyed.

caption.en: Mount Tarawera erupting on 10 June 1886. Painting by Charles Blomfield, based on eyewitness accounts. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The Anglican priest Samuel Marsden arrives from Sydney on the ship Active at Rangihoua in the Bay of Islands on 24 December 1814. The chief Ruatara had agreed that the mission would be on his land. On Christmas Day 1814, at Oihi, Marsden gives the first known Christian sermon on New Zealand soil, and Ruatara explains what the roughly 400 Māori listeners do not understand. It becomes the first station of the Church Missionary Society in the country. The missionaries soon came to trade weapons and ammunition with the Māori for food and goods.

A long series of battles and raids between Māori iwi after the Māori began to acquire muskets. The first known use in fighting between tribes was at Moremonui in 1807. From about 1818 the Ngāpuhi under Hongi Hika attacked tribes across the North Island, and the violence peaked in 1832–1833. In 1835 Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama invaded the Chatham Islands (Rēkohu), killed about a tenth of the Moriori and enslaved the survivors. The wars killed tens of thousands of people and redrew the tribes' boundaries before the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840. The historian Angela Ballara has questioned the term and sees the wars as a continuation of older Māori custom (tikanga), but bloodier because of the weapons.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1806–1845, up to 3,000 battles and 20,000–40,000 dead. Wikidata gives 1807–1842, and Wikipedia's article on the New Zealand Wars writes 1807–1845. Store norske leksikon writes that 30,000–40,000 Māori were killed in more than 600 battles between 1801 and 1840, without using the name Musket Wars. We show Wikipedia's span, 1806–1845. The figures are estimates.

summary.en: On 28 October 1835 chiefs from northern New Zealand sign He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni at Waitangi, in the presence of the British Resident James Busby. They declare the country independent under the name of the United Tribes of New Zealand (Te Wakaminenga o nga Hapu o Nu Tireni), and all power is to rest with the chiefs collectively. The background was concern about lawless British subjects and fear that France would claim the islands. More chiefs signed afterwards, 52 in all by 1839. The document is displayed today at the National Library of New Zealand together with the Treaty of Waitangi.

text.en: Wikipedia says that 34 chiefs signed on 28 October 1835, but the English text reproduced in the same article speaks of 35 signatures.

summary.en: On 21 May 1840 Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson proclaims British sovereignty over New Zealand in two proclamations. The North Island is claimed on the grounds that it was ceded through the Treaty of Waitangi, and the South Island and Stewart Island on the grounds of Cook's discovery in 1769. Two days later he declares illegal the government that the New Zealand Company's settlers had formed at Port Nicholson (Wellington). What the treaty meant for sovereignty is disputed, because the Māori text speaks of kawanatanga, governance.

text.en: Several Wikipedia articles give 21 May 1840, but the article on William Hobson gives 3 May 1840. The Danish encyclopaedia Lex only writes that Hobson annexed New Zealand in 1840. Where the proclamations were issued is not stated in the sources that have been checked, so the place is approximate.

summary.en: By a royal charter of 16 November 1840 the British government decides that New Zealand is to be separated from the colony of New South Wales. On 3 May 1841 the country becomes a separate Crown colony, and Hobson is sworn in as governor. The first organs of government, an Executive Council and a Legislative Council, are established to assist the governor. For many years after 1840 British sovereignty was in practice largely nominal.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 3 May 1841. Wikidata says that the colony began on 1 July 1841. Store norske leksikon writes that New Zealand became a British colony in 1840, and Lex writes in one place that the country was a British colony from 1852.

summary.en: On 30 June 1852 the New Zealand Constitution Act receives royal assent. The act was passed by the British Parliament and gives the colony self-government with representative assemblies. It takes effect when Governor George Grey issues a proclamation on 17 January 1853. The first provincial elections are held in 1853, and Parliament meets for the first time in 1854. The franchise excluded all women, most Māori and everyone who was not British. The act remained part of New Zealand's constitution until it was replaced by the Constitution Act 1986.

In the 1850s the King movement, Kīngitanga, emerges among iwi on the North Island, partly to slow the sale of land to the settlers. The Waikato chief Te Wherowhero accepts in September 1857 and is crowned in June 1858 at Ngāruawāhia, taking the name Pōtatau. Over time the movement acquired its own flag, newspaper (Te Hokioi), laws and magistrates, and the colonial government saw it as a challenge to the British monarchy. It was one of the reasons for the invasion of the Waikato in 1863. Several large iwi, among them Ngāpuhi, Tūhoe and Ngāti Porou, have not joined it. The movement still exists today, with its seat at Tūrangawaewae marae in Ngāruawāhia.

text.en: Wikipedia says that the first king was crowned in 1858, and Wikidata gives 1858 as the year the movement was founded. The Danish encyclopaedia Lex instead describes 1858 as the year the Māori tried to stop the land purchases through an uprising. The month of June comes only from Wikipedia.

summary.en: On 5 November 1863 the New Zealand Settlements Bill is introduced in Parliament, and it becomes law with only two votes against it in each house. The act lets the government take land from tribes regarded as having been in rebellion after 1 January 1863. The land was to become military settlements, and what was left over was to be sold to pay for the war. In practice the confiscations made little distinction between “loyal” and “rebel” tribes. The Waitangi Tribunal and later settlements have taken them up.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the confiscations gives more than 1.2 million hectares, 4.4 per cent of the land, mainly in Waikato, Taranaki and the Bay of Plenty. The article on the New Zealand Wars gives 1.5 million hectares, about 15 per cent of the land then in Māori customary ownership. The day the act came into force is not stated in the sources that have been checked.

summary.en: At the Treaty of Kiel in January 1814, Denmark had to cede Norway to the King of Sweden. Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands, which had previously belonged to Norway, remained with Denmark.

text.en: Lex writes that the peace was signed during the night of 14 to 15 January 1814. Wikipedia gives 14 January.

summary.en: The Malmö–Lund section of the Southern Main Line (Södra stambanan) opens. The railway gave Malmö a new boost and sped up industrialisation in Lund.

In December 1865 the Riksdag of the Estates decided to abolish representation by estates, and the reform came into force on 22 June 1866. Instead Sweden got a parliament with two chambers, where the second chamber was chosen in direct elections. The driving force was the Minister of Justice, Louis De Geer.

From the 1840s to the 1920s, around 1.25–1.3 million Swedes emigrated to the United States. Emigration came in several waves and was greatest in 1870–1900. The famine years of 1867–1869 set it going. Most travelled from Gothenburg by boat to Hull in England and on by train to Liverpool, where the ships crossed the Atlantic. In 1890 the US census counted nearly 800,000 Swedish Americans.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on Swedish emigration to the United States gives about 1.3 million in the 19th and early 20th centuries. The article on the famine years gives about 1.25 million from the 1860s to the 1920s.

caption.en: Emigrants in Gothenburg boarding the steamer Calypso of the Wilson Line for the journey to England and America, 1905. One half of a stereo photograph, detail. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: In 1867–1869 Sweden was struck by famine, worst in parts of northern Sweden such as Västerbotten County. The drought of 1868 caused crop failure and starving animals, and epidemics followed. About 10,000 people died. The famine contributed to emigration: about 60,000 Swedes left for the United States in those years.

On 13 October 1804 the Japanese physician Hanaoka Seishū removed part of the breast of Kan Aiya, a 60-year-old woman with breast cancer. She was put to sleep with the anaesthetic tsūsensan. According to the source, some today regard the operation as the first reliably documented operation under general anaesthesia.

On 16 October 1846 the dentist William T. G. Morton put the patient Edward Gilbert Abbott to sleep with ether at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. The surgeon John Collins Warren then removed part of a tumour. It was the first public demonstration of ether as an anaesthetic for surgery. The source gives two places for the tumour: the neck and the left side of the jaw.

In 1847 the physician Ignaz Semmelweis proposed that staff at the First Obstetrical Clinic of Vienna General Hospital should wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime. Maternal mortality at the clinic fell from 18 per cent to under 2 per cent. Even so, his ideas were rejected by the medical community.

caption.en: Ignaz Semmelweis. Copperplate engraving by Jenő Doby, 1894. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 31 August 1854 a severe cholera outbreak began around Broad Street in Soho, London. In the first three days 127 people died, and by the end 420 had died. The physician John Snow traced the infection to the public water pump in the street, and after he had met the parish board, the pump's handle was removed. The outbreak may already have been declining. The source calls Snow's study the founding event of epidemiology.

caption.en: John Snow's map of the cholera around Broad Street in Soho in 1854. The cases are marked in black. Detail. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 12 August 1865 the surgeon Joseph Lister succeeded for the first time in treating a patient with carbolic acid, after two attempts in March of the same year that did not succeed: eleven-year-old James Greenlees, who had an open fracture of his left leg. The bone healed without suppuration. In 1867 Lister described the method in the journal The Lancet. According to the source, his work reduced infections after operations and made surgery safer for patients.

caption.en: Lister's carbolic spray in use during an operation. Image from the book Antiseptic surgery from 1882, seventeen years after Lister's first successful treatment with carbolic acid. Licence: CC BY 4.0.

summary.en: In 1881 the Cuban epidemiologist Carlos Finlay became the first to put forward the theory that yellow fever is spread by a mosquito, of the genus Aedes. The theory was confirmed nearly twenty years later, by the Walter Reed Commission in 1900.

text.en: According to the main text of the source, Finlay put forward the theory at the 1881 International Sanitary Conference, which was held in Washington. A footnote in the same source says that the paper was presented on 14 August 1881 and printed in 1882 in a journal of the academy of sciences in Havana (Real Academia de Ciencias Médicas, Físicas y Naturales de la Habana). The globe shows Havana.

summary.en: On 24 March 1882 Robert Koch presented his discovery of the tuberculosis bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, to the German Physiological Society in Berlin. Since 1982 the World Health Organization has marked the day as World Tuberculosis Day. Koch received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1905 for his work on tuberculosis.

caption.en: Robert Koch and his wife, photographed around 1908 according to the Bain News Service, 26 years after the discovery. The Library of Congress states no known restrictions on publication.

summary.en: On 20 August 1897 the physician Ronald Ross found the malaria parasite inside a mosquito, in a building in Begumpet, Secunderabad. The discovery showed that malaria is spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes. The day is now marked as World Mosquito Day, and Ross received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1902.

On 6 June 1809 King Charles XIII signs a new Instrument of Government. It gives the Riksdag power over taxation and makes the king’s ministers answerable to the Riksdag. It remained in force until 1 January 1975 and in its final years was one of the oldest written constitutions still in force in the world.

On 26 September 1832 the Göta Canal opens after 22 years of work. The canal is about 190 kilometres long, has 58 locks and links Lake Vänern with the Baltic Sea. The driving force was Baltzar von Platen.

On 6 April 1830 Joseph Smith, Oliver Cowdery and about 30 believers met to formally organise the Church of Christ. It was the first organisation built on the Book of Mormon, which Smith had just published, and it counts as the beginning of the Latter Day Saint movement. From 1829 believers in three towns in New York State had already called themselves the Church of Christ. Later names included the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints.

text.en: The source says it is uncertain where the meeting was held: in the home of Peter Whitmer Sr. in Fayette, or in the log home of Joseph Smith Sr. in Manchester. The point is at Fayette.

summary.en: On the evening of 22 May 1844 the merchant ʻAlí-Muḥammad invited Mullá Husayn to his house in Shiraz and told him of his mission. Mullá Husayn became the first to accept his claims. ʻAlí-Muḥammad called himself the Báb, “the gate”, and founded Bábism. He wrote that his task was to prepare for an even greater messenger. The clergy and the government turned against him, and in 1850 he was executed in Tabriz. The Báb is also one of the central figures of the Baháʼí Faith.

On 15 March 1877 a match began at the Melbourne Cricket Ground between a combined Australian team and James Lillywhite’s team of English professionals. Australia won by 45 runs. The match now counts as the first Test match, but that status was given afterwards: Test cricket only became an officially recognised format in the 1890s, and matches between Australia and England were called Test matches from 1892.

text.en: The match was given Test status afterwards. It was not called that when it was played.
